paragraphs: This ceaseless agitation, which democratic government has introduced into the political world, spreads into all of social life. I am not sure that, on the whole, this is not the greatest advantage of democracy. I am also much less inclined to praise democracy for what it does than for what it causes to be done. It cannot be denied that the people often conduct public business very badly. But the lower classes cannot take part in public business without widening the circle of their ideas and stepping outside the ordinary routine of their minds. The humblest person who is called on to help govern society gains a certain self-respect. Because he holds authority, he can command the services of minds far more educated than his own. A crowd of petitioners courts him and tries to deceive him in a thousand different ways, yet they instruct him by their very deceit. He takes part in political undertakings that he did not conceive himself, but that give him a taste for undertakings of that kind. Every day, improvements are pointed out in the property he holds in common with others, and this gives him a desire to improve the property that is more especially his own. He is perhaps neither happier nor better than those who came before him, but he is better informed and more active. I have no doubt that the democratic institutions of the United States, together with the physical character of the country, are the cause of the prodigious commercial activity of its inhabitants. They are not the direct cause, as is so often asserted, but the indirect one. The laws do not produce this activity, but the people learn how to promote it from their experience of making laws.

When the opponents of democracy say that a single individual carries out the tasks he takes on much better than the government of the community does, it seems to me that they are perfectly right. Where the two sides are equally well informed, the government of one person is more consistent, more persevering and more accurate than that of a multitude. It is also much better able to judge wisely the characters of the men it employs. Anyone who denies this has certainly never seen a democratic government, or has formed his opinion on very partial evidence. It is true that even when local circumstances and the disposition of the people allow democratic institutions to survive, they never display a regular and methodical system of government. Democratic liberty is far from carrying out all the projects it undertakes with the skill of an adroit despotism. It often abandons them before they have borne fruit, or risks them when the consequences may prove dangerous. But in the end it produces more than any absolute government does: if it does fewer things well, it does a greater number of things. Under its rule, what the public administration accomplishes is not nearly so important as what private effort accomplishes. Democracy does not give the people the most skillful kind of government, but it produces something that the most skillful governments are often unable to awaken, namely an all-pervading and restless activity, an overflowing force, and an energy that cannot be separated from it and that may, under favorable circumstances, give rise to the most amazing benefits. These are the true advantages of democracy.

In the present age, when the destinies of Christendom seem to hang in the balance, some people hurry to attack democracy as an enemy while it is still in its early growth. Others are ready with vows of worship for this new deity rising out of chaos. But both parties know very little about the object of their hatred or of their desire. They strike in the dark and land their blows by pure chance.

We must first understand what the purpose of society and the aim of government are taken to be. Suppose you intend to raise the human mind to a certain height and to teach it to look on the things of this world with generous feelings. Suppose you want to inspire in people a scorn for mere material advantage, to give birth to living convictions, and to keep alive the spirit of honorable devotion. Suppose you think it good to refine a nation’s habits, to improve its manners, to cultivate its arts, and to promote the love of poetry, of beauty and of renown. Suppose you want to form a people able to act with power on all other nations, and prepared for those high enterprises that, whatever the outcome of its efforts, will leave a name famous for all time. If you believe that these are the principal objects of society, you must avoid the government of democracy, which would be a very uncertain guide to the end you have in view.

But suppose you think it more useful to turn the moral and intellectual activity of man toward producing comfort and acquiring the necessities of life. Suppose you think a clear understanding is more profitable to man than genius. Suppose your aim is not to stimulate the virtues of heroism but to create habits of peace. Suppose you would rather see vices than crimes, and are content to find fewer noble deeds provided that offenses are reduced in the same proportion. Suppose that, instead of living in the midst of a brilliant society, you are content to have prosperity around you. Suppose, in short, that you hold the principal object of a government to be not to give the greatest possible share of power and glory to the nation as a body, but to ensure the greatest enjoyment and the least misery to each of the individuals who make it up. If such are your desires, you can have no surer means of satisfying them than to make conditions equal among men and to establish democratic institutions.

But suppose the time when such a choice was possible has passed, and some superhuman power drives us toward one or the other of these two kinds of government without consulting our wishes. Then let us at least try to make the best of the one that has been assigned to us. Let us examine its good and its evil tendencies closely enough that we can encourage the good and hold the evil in check as far as we can.
